page: Amazon Web Services i4g.2xlarge is a storage-optimized server instance powered by the AWS Graviton processor family. It features 8 dedicated physical cores on the ARM64 architecture, utilizing the AWS Neoverse-N1 model running at 2.5 GHz. The instance is equipped with 64.0 GB of system memory, providing 8.0 GB of RAM per core. Local storage is bundled, consisting of a 1875 GB NVMe SSD, and network performance is anchored by a 5 Gbps baseline bandwidth. The instance runs on the AWS Nitro hypervisor.

Benchmark results indicate average performance across several key metrics, alongside notable weak points. The stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU tests fall into the average range, with scores of 1519.59 and 12132.09 respectively. Memory bandwidth is robust, reaching 472.81 GB/sec for cached small-block reads and 116.33 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads. However, single-threaded operations show limitations; the Geekbench single-core score of 937.0 and the Passmark CPU score of 5246.06 are categorized as weak. Cryptographic and compression tasks also represent a performance bottleneck, with bzip3 single-threaded decompression scoring in the poor range at 7.19 GB/sec and the Passmark CPU encryption test scoring 1086.33.

Given the 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio and the integrated 1875 GB NVMe SSD, the i4g.2xlarge offers a balanced profile for storage-heavy and database workloads. It achieves an average score of 5224.61 in Passmark database operations and processes 9.8 million operations per second in Redis SET benchmarks. Static web serving throughput is also average at 9.71 GB/sec. Conversely, the instance is less suited for intensive computational tasks, such as large-scale LLM inference, where text generation speeds for a 7B model drop to 6.74 tokens per second. From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the ARM-based architecture provides a dense configuration of memory and local NVMe storage, making it a viable option for database hosting, caching layers, and web serving where high-speed local storage is required without the premium of x86 licensing.
